In summary, our research is concerned with

the production, purification, and characterization of anti-HER IgA antibodies, including the effect of N-glycan modifications on the in vitro and in vivo efficacy, and the potential of IgA as an antibody class for cancer therapy.
the production, purification, glycosylation analysis, functional characterization and in vivo evaluation of IgA1 and IgA subclasses 2m1 and 2m2 as anti-cancer antibody therapeutics.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IgA1 antibodies are not suitable for anti-cancer therapy, whereas the IgG1 and IgA1 isotypes are equally potent in terms of ADCC, and IgA2 antibodies have a higher in vivo efficacy than IgG1.
the IgA2 subtype, in contrast to IgA1, is an attractive antibody format for cancer immunotherapy.
the anti-HER antibody IgA1 and IgA1m1 antibodies are not good alternatives for IgG1 in cancer therapy due to their low efficacy in vitro, in vivo and in the clinic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anti-HER2 monomeric IgA2m antibodies are promising candidates for anti-cancer therapy, but that their in vivo potency can be improved by increasing sialylation and/or by reducing polymerization.
anti-HER2 monomeric IgA antibodies have the potential to be used as cancer therapeutics.
anti-HER2 mIgA2m2 is a promising candidate for further development as an anti-cancer agent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the in vivo efficacy of anti-HER IgA antibodies can be improved by increasing the plasma half-life of IgA antibodies and the F(ab')2 potency of the antibody.
the in vivo efficacy of IgA antibodies is highly dependent on their sialylation status, with the most pronounced effect on the in vivo half-life.
IgA2m isotype and sialylation are key determinants in the efficacy of anti-HER IgA antibodies.
